Shamefully
shām'foŏl-lĭ
adv. (disgracefully; with insult and dishonour; rendering Hebrew bosh and Greek atimazo and hubrizo)
Old English scamu, shame, with the adverbial ending. The Greek hubrizo behind 1 Thessalonians 2:2 gives us hubris: to treat a man with insolent outrage.

Biblical Definition

Hosea uses the word of Israel herself: “their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully” (Hos 2:5), and the shame is not embarrassment but covenant adultery — going after lovers who she supposed gave her bread and water, wool and flax. In the parable of the vineyard the word describes what tenants do to a lord's messengers: they cast stones at one and “sent him away shamefully handled” (Mar 12:4), and Luke's parallel says they “entreated him shamefully, and sent him away empty” (Luk 20:11). This is the settled treatment of the prophets, and the parable is heading somewhere: last of all he sent unto them his son. Paul then applies the same verb to his own ministry: “after that we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated, as ye know, at Philippi, we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention” (1Th 2:2). The Greek there is hubrizo — the beating and the inner prison and the stocks, done to a Roman citizen without trial. Paul mentions it not to be pitied but to prove a point: shameful handling did not stop the message, and the Thessalonians had the gospel because it did not.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines shamefully as disgracefully; in a manner to bring reproach; with indignity; and, in an older use, infamously.

expand to see more

SHAMEFULLY, adv. Disgracefully; in a manner to bring reproach.

2. With indignity or indecency; in a manner that may cause shame.

SHAMEFUL, a. That brings shame or disgrace; scandalous; disgraceful; injurious to reputation.

Key Scripture

Hos 2:5 — "For their mother hath played the harlot: she that conceived them hath done shamefully: for she said, I will go after my lovers, that give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, mine oil and my drink."

Luk 20:11 — "And again he sent another servant: and they beat him also, and entreated him shamefully, and sent him away empty."

1Th 2:2 — "But even after that we had suffered before, and were shamefully entreated, as ye know, at Philippi, we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God with much contention."

Modern Corruption

Shame is now treated as a purely social injury to be dismantled, so that the biblical distinction between the shame a man ought to feel for sin and the shame unjustly heaped on him for righteousness is lost.

expand to see more

Scripture knows three shames and keeps them apart. There is the shame that belongs to sin and ought to be felt — Hosea's Israel has done shamefully, and Jeremiah's complaint against his generation is that they were not at all ashamed, neither could they blush. There is the shame unjustly inflicted on the faithful — Paul shamefully entreated at Philippi, the servants of the vineyard sent away empty. And there is the shame Christ despised on the cross, borne for others. The modern account collapses all three into one category to be eliminated, on the assumption that shame as such is an injury done by society to the self. The result is that a man who ought to be ashamed is taught that his shame is a wound inflicted on him, while a church shamefully entreated for the gospel is taught to regard the treatment as a failure of its own public relations. Paul's response at Thessalonica is the corrective, and it is entirely unsentimental: we were shamefully entreated, and we were bold in our God to speak unto you the gospel of God. The shame was real, it was unjust, and it changed nothing about the errand.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bosh (H954), to be ashamed, to be confounded; Greek atimazo (G818), to dishonour, to treat with contempt; Greek hubrizo (G5195), to treat insolently, to outrage.

expand to see more

Hebrew bosh (H954) — to be ashamed, confounded, disappointed; the covenant word for Israel's harlotry and for the hope that never fails; Hosea 2:5, Psalm 25:3.

Greek atimazo (G818) — to dishonour, to treat as without honour; the vineyard servants and the apostles counted worthy to suffer it; Mark 12:4, Acts 5:41.

Greek hubrizo (G5195) — to treat with insolent outrage; the beating and stocks at Philippi, and the Lord's own foretelling of His passion; 1 Thessalonians 2:2, Luke 18:32.

Usage

"“She that conceived them hath done shamefully” — the shame that belongs to covenant unfaithfulness."

"“Entreated him shamefully, and sent him away empty” — the standing treatment of the prophets, and the parable's warning."

"“Shamefully entreated…we were bold in our God” — Philippi did not silence Thessalonica."
